I will identify the causal effect using instrumental variables that exploit the 1992 randomized village draw: instrument log household income per adult equivalent with the interaction of transfer_draw and a post‑1992 indicator in a panel 2SLS / difference‑in‑differences framework, including individual and survey‑round fixed effects and clustering standard errors at the village level. The outcome is the respondent's count of illness episodes in the prior four weeks; the endogenous regressor is log household income per adult equivalent; key controls include age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, land_acres and season_rain (and I will test robustness to additional covariates). I will estimate a linear FE 2SLS as the primary specification for transparent interpretation and report complementary IV‑Poisson and IV‑negative‑binomial estimates to respect the count nature of the outcome. I will test the identifying assumptions with balance and pre‑trend tests on pre‑1992 rounds, placebo outcomes, and heterogeneity checks, and I will examine attrition and spillovers across villages. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the village draw affected health through channels other than household income (local public goods, health services, malaria exposure, or other programmatic changes) or induced differential attrition; I will therefore control for observable village‑level shocks (season_rain), run village‑level placebo checks, and bound estimates using alternative specifications.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
transfer_draw*post | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw*post

I will estimate the causal effect using the 1992 randomized village draw as an instrument in a panel IV / difference-in-differences design: use transfer_draw (village-level random assignment to quarterly unconditional cash transfers) as the instrument for log household income per adult equivalent, exploiting the four-round panel with individual and survey-round fixed effects. The first stage regresses log household income on transfer_draw (and fixed effects); the second stage regresses the individual's reported number of illness episodes in the prior four weeks on the predicted income from the first stage, clustering standard errors at the village level and using wild-cluster bootstrap given 51 clusters. Key variables are transfer_draw (instrument), log household income per adult equivalent (treatment), illness episodes in last four weeks (outcome), individual and round fixed effects, and controls like age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic and land_acres to improve precision. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the transfer changed other village-level inputs or behaviors that directly affect health (spillovers, changes in health service provision or care-seeking) or differential attrition/noncompliance; small number of clusters and measurement error in income also risk weak-instrument or inference problems. I will test threats with balance checks and pre-trend/placebo tests, estimate the reduced-form effect of transfer_draw on health, control for time-varying season_rain, and report IV, reduced-form, and intent-to-treat estimates plus sensitivity bounds.  

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect with an instrumental-variables design: use the 1992 randomized village draw (transfer_draw) interacted with a post‑1992 indicator as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent and estimate the effect on four‑week reported illness episodes by two‑stage least squares. The main equation will include individual and survey‑round fixed effects, cluster standard errors at the village level, and baseline covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic) to improve precision; I will also report first‑stage F and run IV‑Poisson as a robustness check. The program memo states the fund changed nothing else in drawn villages and raised log income by ~0.12 on average, supporting relevance and (plausibly) exclusion, but I will test for pre‑trend differences and check for migration or service changes using administrative indicators. The primary threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the transfer affected health through channels other than income (e.g., in‑kind changes, health services, differential reporting, or spillovers to neighboring villages) or if treated villages experienced other concurrent shocks. I will therefore present robustness checks: (a) balance and pre‑trend tests, (b) alternate specifications excluding villages near treated ones to reduce spillovers, and (c) placebo IVs and falsification outcomes unrelated to income.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares where the instrument is the 1992 random village draw interacted with a post-draw indicator, exploiting panel variation from interviews before and after the draw and including individual and survey-round fixed effects. The first stage regresses log household income per adult equivalent on transfer_draw × Post and covariates; the second stage regresses the number of illness episodes in the prior four weeks on predicted income. Key variables are outcome = illness episode count, treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, instrument = transfer_draw × Post, with controls (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic) and clustered SEs at the village level. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the transfer changed health through channels other than income (direct health spending, programs, migration or local spillovers), or if drawn villages experienced different pre-trends; I will check pre-draw balance, first-stage strength, and placebo tests on pre-draw rounds. I will report IV, reduced-form, and OLS estimates plus sensitivity analyses (e.g., adding controls, bounding, and alternative clustering).

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
transfer_draw×Post | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw×Post

I will estimate the causal effect using the 1992 randomized village draw (transfer_draw) as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent in a two-stage least squares panel design, exploiting repeated interviews with individual and survey-round fixed effects and village-clustered standard errors. Key variables are: instrument = transfer_draw; endogenous treatment = log household income per adult equivalent; outcome = number of illness episodes reported in the prior four weeks; I will include baseline covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, land_acres, season_rain) to improve precision. I will report the first-stage F-statistic (the draw raised log income by about 0.12 on average) and interpret the 2SLS estimate as the LATE for compliers whose income changed because their village was drawn. The main threat to identification is violation of the exclusion restriction or interference—transfer_draw could affect health through channels other than household income (local spillovers, changes in public goods, differential migration or reporting), or differential attrition/measurement error correlated with the draw. I will mitigate these threats with balance and pre-trend tests, village-by-round fixed effects and placebo outcomes, and sensitivity analyses.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect by instrumenting log household income per adult equivalent with the 1992 randomized village draw for unconditional cash transfers (transfer_draw), implementing two-stage least squares on the person-panel and exploiting timing across survey rounds (i.e., transfer_draw × post-draw exposure) so variation is randomized at the village level. The outcome is individual-reported illness episodes in the prior four weeks; key variables are the outcome, the treatment log household income per adult equivalent, the instrument transfer_draw (and its interaction with post-draw rounds), individual and survey-round fixed effects, and baseline covariates (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic) for precision. I will cluster standard errors at the village level, report ITT and IV (LATE) estimates, check first-stage F-statistics, and run IV-appropriate count-model robustness (e.g., control-function/IV-Poisson) because the outcome is a count. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction: the transfers might affect health through channels other than household income (community spillovers, changes in local service provision, or altered reporting), or cause differential migration/attrition correlated with assignment. I will assess balance and pre-trends, test for spillovers by distance/subsample, and treat season_rain and dist_clinic as controls/sensitivity checks rather than instruments.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | doubtful
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will identify the causal effect by instrumenting log household income per adult equivalent with the 1992 random village draw for unconditional transfers (transfer_draw interacted with a post-draw indicator) and estimate by 2SLS in panel form with individual and survey‑round fixed effects and village‑clustered standard errors. The main variables are: outcome = number of illness episodes in the prior four weeks; endogenous regressor = log household income per adult equivalent; instrument = transfer_draw × post‑draw; controls = age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, season_rain and survey‑round fixed effects. Because the outcome is a count I will present linear IV estimates (for LATE) and as a robustness check estimate an IV‑Poisson or control‑function approach to recover incidence rate effects, always reporting the first‑stage F. I will test the identifying assumption with pre‑trend/placebo tests on pre‑draw rounds, balance checks on baseline covariates, and checks for differential attrition or reporting and for spillovers to nearby villages. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the fund or the draw changed other village‑level services, reporting behavior, or induced spillovers (so the instrument affects health through channels other than household income).  
CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | doubtful
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect by using transfer_draw (the 1992 randomized village draw that raised household log income by about 0.12) as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent in a two-stage least-squares specification, exploiting the randomized cross-village variation and including individual and survey-round fixed effects. Key variables are: treatment = log household income per adult equivalent, outcome = number of self-reported illness episodes in the four weeks before interview, instrument = transfer_draw, and covariates for precision/robustness including age, female, educ_years, hh_size, dist_clinic, land_acres and season_rain. I will cluster standard errors at the village level, report first-stage F-statistics, run balance tests on pre-draw observables and placebo outcomes, and present both IV and reduced-form (intent-to-treat) estimates with heterogeneity by baseline vulnerability and migration. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction or contamination: if the transfers changed health through channels other than household income (e.g., direct health-related programs, in-kind provision, increased clinic use, migration, or social spillovers) or if draw assignment/migration produced nonrandom exposure across households. If transfer_draw fails validity/strength checks I will transparently report ITT results and sensitivity analyses rather than rely on a weaker or plausibly invalid instrument.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | violated
dist_clinic | violated
land_acres | doubtful
assets_amou_046 | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

Use the 1992 randomized village draw as an instrument for log household income per adult equivalent and estimate the causal effect on reported illness episodes via two-stage least squares (2SLS), including individual and survey‑round fixed effects and clustering standard errors at the village level. Key variables: outcome = number of illness episodes in the prior four weeks; treatment = log household income per adult equivalent; instrument = transfer_draw; include pre-treatment controls (age, female, educ_years, hh_size, land_acres, dist_clinic, season_rain) and baseline covariates for precision. Estimate and report the first-stage F-stat, run robustness checks using IV-Poisson or control‑function approaches for count data, and report heterogeneity and intention-to-treat estimates. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction or SUTVA: the cash transfers may have affected health through non-income channels (local services, prices, social networks) or caused migration/spillovers that correlate with health. Mitigate by testing pre-draw balance, testing for village-level spillovers (non-recipient households), placebo instruments (e.g., season_rain), and sensitivity analyses excluding villages with observable post-draw changes in services.

CANDIDATES:
transfer_draw | plausible
season_rain | doubtful
dist_clinic | violated
INSTRUMENT: transfer_draw

I will estimate the causal effect with two-stage least squares (2SLS), using the district’s randomized elective-credit waiver (credit_waiver) as an instrument for graduating from high school by age 19 to recover a LATE for compliers. The outcome is the binary indicator “voted in at least one general election 1998–2008” and the endogenous regressor is “graduated by age 19.” I will report the first-stage relationship (expect ~14 percentage-point increase) and F-statistics, present the IV estimate alongside the ITT, and use weak-instrument–robust inference (e.g., Anderson–Rubin) and exact finite-sample checks given n=123. I will include pre-treatment covariates (female, birth_year, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home) only to improve precision and run sensitivity checks for alternative samples and specification. The main threat is that credit_waiver is observed only for students who reached 12th grade (selection/attrition and restricted instrument support) and could violate exclusion if the waiver affected turnout through channels other than enabling graduation or if small-sample/weak-instrument problems bias inference.
CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect with an instrumental-variables design (2SLS), using the randomized elective-credit waiver (credit_waiver) as the instrument for graduating from high school by age 19 and report both the ITT (reduced form) and the LATE for compliers. I will restrict the analysis to participants who reached 12th grade (the universe in which credit_waiver was randomized), present first-stage strength (F-stat) and weak-IV–robust confidence intervals given the small sample, and use robust standard errors. Key variables: instrument = credit_waiver; endogenous treatment = graduated_by19; outcome = voted_at_least_once_1998_2008 (from voter files); baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year, father_home) will be included for precision and balance checks only. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction (the waiver could influence turnout through channels other than graduation, or randomization may be compromised by selective survival/matching to the voter file), plus limited power from N=123 and possible weak instrument behavior in subgroups. I will do robustness checks using the preschool assignment (preschool_assign) as an alternative instrument but treat any estimate with that instrument as suspect because the early program plausibly had direct long-term effects on civic behavior.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect via two-stage least squares (2SLS), using the district's randomized senior-year elective-credit waiver as an instrument for graduating from high school by age 19. I will restrict to students who reached 12th grade (for whom credit_waiver is defined), run a first-stage of graduation_on_credit_waiver (+ baseline covariates for precision: female, iq_entry, parent_educ, father_home, ses_index, birth_year), and a second-stage of voted_in_1998_2008_on_predicted_graduation; report first-stage F, IV point estimate, and weak-instrument robust CIs. Key variables: treatment = graduated by age 19, outcome = voted at least once in general elections 1998–2008 (voter-file), instrument = credit_waiver, with baseline covariates to improve precision. The identifying assumption is that credit_waiver was randomly assigned among seniors and affects adult turnout only through its effect on graduation (so 2SLS estimates a LATE for compliers). The main threat is that the instrument is defined only for seniors so estimates generalize only to that subgroup and could be biased if the waiver affected turnout through other unobserved channels or induced selection into the analysis, compounded by the small sample and potential weak-instrument problems.
CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | violated
credit_waiver | plausible
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect using random-assignment variation: instrument the binary indicator for graduating high school by age 19 with assignment to two years of the district's randomized half-day preschool (preschool_assign) and report two-stage least squares LATE estimates together with weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals and randomization-inference p-values. Key variables are the treatment (graduated high school by 19), the outcome (voted in at least one general election, 1998–2008, from matched voter files), and the instrument (preschool_assign); I will include baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home, birth_year) for precision and to check balance. I will report first-stage strength (F-statistic and the estimated 19 percentage-point effect on graduation), present the ITT (preschool assignment → voting) and IV estimates, and use randomization inference keyed to the original assignment to obtain exact p-values given the small sample. The primary threat is violation of the exclusion restriction (preschool_assign may affect adult voting through channels other than high‑school graduation — e.g., civic skills, networks, long-run socioeconomic changes) and possible differential matching to the voter file by assignment; small sample imprecision and LATE interpretation (compliers only) are additional concerns. To probe these threats I will test balance and the effect of assignment on intermediate outcomes (employment, arrests, family/welfare indicators) and, as a robustness check, use the randomized credit_waiver draw as a secondary instrument among those who reached 12th grade and report sensitivity analyses.  
CANDIDATES:
preschool_assign | plausible
credit_waiver | plausible
INSTRUMENT: preschool_assign

I will estimate the causal effect using instrumental variables (2SLS), instrumenting graduation by age 19 with the district's randomized credit_waiver draw (a randomized waiver among seniors that raised graduation by ≈14 percentage points) to recover a local average treatment effect for compliers. Key variables are graduated_by_19 (treatment), voted_1998_2008 (binary outcome from voter files), credit_waiver (instrument), and baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year) included for precision and balance checks. Because credit_waiver is defined only for students who reached 12th grade I will restrict the primary IV sample to that universe, report ITT estimates by draw, present first-stage F-statistics and Stock–Yogo weak-instrument checks, and use robust inference appropriate for the small sample (N=123). The main identifying assumption is that the randomized waiver affected later voting only through enabling graduation (exclusion restriction) and not via other channels; the principal threat is violation of that exclusion or selection bias introduced by conditioning on reaching 12th grade (and limited power). For robustness I will (a) run balance tests, (b) repeat analyses using preschool_assign as a secondary instrument or robustness check while noting its greater risk of direct effects on turnout, and (c) report LATE interpretation and sensitivity/bounds for exclusion violations. I will transparently report precision limits and emphasize LATE interpretation given the sample and sample restrictions.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect with two-stage least squares (IV): use the district's randomized credit-waiver draw (credit_waiver) as the instrument for graduating from high school by age 19 to recover a LATE among students who reached 12th grade. Key variables are credit_waiver (instrument), graduated_by_19 (treatment), voted_any_1998_2008 (outcome: voted in at least one general election 1998–2008), and baseline covariates for precision (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year). I will restrict the primary analysis to participants with nonmissing credit_waiver (i.e., reached 12th grade), demonstrate a strong first stage (report F-statistic), and show balance of baseline covariates by instrument. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction or post-treatment pathways: the waiver might affect turnout through senior-year engagement, peer networks, administrative record differences that affect voter-file matching, or other channels besides graduation, and restricting to 12th graders may induce selection bias. I will present weak-instrument–robust CIs, OLS and IV point estimates, and sensitivity checks using preschool_assign as an alternative instrument and intent-to-treat estimates from the preschool randomization.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate a local average treatment effect of graduating by age 19 on adult turnout using two-stage least squares (first stage: graduated_by19 ~ credit_waiver + covariates; second stage: voted_any_1998_2008 ~ predicted_graduation + covariates), interpreting the estimate as the effect for seniors induced to graduate by the waiver. Key variables are the randomized senior credit-waiver (credit_waiver) as the instrument, the endogenous treatment graduated_by19, and the outcome indicator constructed from the voter-file (voted_any_1998_2008); I will include baseline covariates (female, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, birth_year) for precision. I will report first-stage strength (F-statistic), the ITT, the 2SLS LATE, and clustered SEs, and I will pre-specify balance and placebo checks and a bounded-sensitivity analysis for violations of exclusion. Identification rests on random assignment of the waiver among 12th-grade students and the exclusion restriction that the waiver "changed nothing else" except graduation; monotonicity is assumed (no one is less likely to graduate because of the waiver). The main threat is violation of exclusion (the waiver could plausibly change unobserved schooling experiences or civic engagement that affect turnout) and sample-selection/matching bias because the instrument is defined only for students who reached 12th grade and voter-file linkage may be differential; I will assess robustness by ITT estimates, by adding pre-treatment controls, and by using preschool_assign as a placebo/secondary instrument check. Results will be framed as LATE for compliers (students induced to graduate by the waiver) and accompanied by weak-instrument and sensitivity diagnostics.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect of graduating from high school by age 19 on adult voter turnout using instrumental variables: the district's randomized draw that waived one elective credit (credit_waiver) will serve as the instrument for graduation, giving a 2SLS LATE for compliers who reached 12th grade. Key variables are instrument = credit_waiver, endogenous treatment = graduated_high_school_by_19, outcome = voted_in_any_general_1998_2008 (voter-file match), and baseline covariates (female, birth_year, iq_entry, parent_educ, ses_index, father_home) used for precision and balance checks. I will restrict the primary IV analysis to the subsample that reached 12th grade (credit_waiver observed), report first-stage strength (expect ~14 ppt increase in graduation; require F>10), the ITT, and 2SLS estimates with robust SEs, and present OLS for comparison. Validity checks include pre-treatment balance tests by credit_waiver, placebo outcomes (baseline test scores, early arrests), heterogeneity analyses, and a sensitivity check using preschool_assign for comparison. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction (or nonrandom missingness of credit_waiver): if the waiver affected turnout through channels other than obtaining a diploma, the IV estimate will be biased and applies only to compliers.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect using instrumental variables (2SLS), exploiting the district's randomized elective-credit waiver draw as an instrument for graduating from high school by age 19 and restricting the sample to students who reached 12th grade (credit_waiver is missing otherwise). Key variables are: treatment = graduated from high school by age 19; outcome = voted in at least one general election from 1998–2008 (voter-file match); instrument = credit_waiver; baseline covariates for precision include female, birth_year, iq_entry, parent_educ, father_home, and ses_index. First stage: regress graduation on credit_waiver and covariates and report first-stage F-statistics; second stage: regress turnout on predicted graduation, using robust and weak-instrument–robust inference (e.g., Anderson–Rubin/LIML). This estimates a local average treatment effect for compliers (those whose graduation was affected by the waiver) and I will report the sample restrictions and complier interpretation. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the waiver affected later turnout through channels other than graduation (or if the draw was not perfectly random), plus selection (instrument only defined among twelfth-graders) and low power with N=123.

CANDIDATES:
credit_waiver | plausible
preschool_assign | violated
INSTRUMENT: credit_waiver

I will estimate the causal effect of racial segregation on city per‑resident direct general expenditure using the 1990 randomized fair‑housing testing grant draw as an instrument for the city segregation entropy index and implement two‑stage least squares in the 1980–2010 panel. The first stage regresses the segregation index on audit_grant, controlling for log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region, city fixed effects and state‑by‑year fixed effects; the second stage regresses per‑resident direct general expenditure on the instrumented segregation value with clustered standard errors. Key variables are the multigroup entropy segregation index (treatment), direct general expenditure per resident (outcome), audit_grant (instrument), and the listed demographic and economic controls plus state‑by‑year FEs and city FEs to absorb time‑invariant city characteristics and common shocks. I will check instrument strength (F‑statistic) and test robustness to including waterways and other geographic controls, and estimate local average treatment effects by cohort if compliance varies over time. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the randomized grant affected municipal spending through channels other than segregation (e.g., sustained NGO activity, political attention) or if the instrument is weak given its modest impact on segregation. If IV assumptions fail, I will report bounds and supplement with fixed‑effects DiD exploiting pre/post changes in segregation concentrated in drawn vs. undrawn cities.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | doubtful
audit_grant | plausible
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate the causal effect using two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumenting the city segregation entropy index with the 1990 federal fair‑housing testing random draw (audit_grant), exploiting the panel of cities with city and year (or state-by-year) fixed effects and clustering SEs by city. The first stage will regress segregation on audit_grant and pre‑treatment covariates for precision (log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate) and state‑by‑year fixed effects; the second stage will regress direct general expenditure per resident (real dollars) on the predicted segregation from the first stage. Key variables: treatment = segregation entropy index (0–100), outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (deflated), instrument = audit_grant, controls = log_pop plus baseline demographic/economic covariates and state-by-year FEs. Main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the grant affected municipal spending through channels other than segregation (e.g., political mobilization, litigation, external funding, or differential measurement/selection); I will run balance and placebo tests on pre‑1990 outcomes, check first‑stage strength (F‑stat), and report sensitivity bounds. If exclusion appears violated or instrument weak, I will report reduced‑form estimates and bounds rather than a causal IV estimate.

CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | plausible
waterways | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I'll estimate the causal effect using 2SLS in the city panel, instrumenting the city's segregation index with assignment to the 1990 federal fair‑housing testing grant (audit_grant), exploiting the random draw and pre/post variation across the 1980/1990/2000/2010 censuses; first stage: segregation_it = γ0 + γ1*(audit_grant_i × post1990_t) + X_it + δ_state×year + α_i + ε_it, second stage: expenditure_pc_it = β0 + β1*predicted_segregation_it + X_it + δ_state×year + α_i + υ_it. Key variables are segregation (multigroup entropy 0–100) as treatment, direct general expenditure per resident (inflation‑adjusted) as the outcome, audit_grant as the instrument (with audit_grant×post indicators as needed), and controls log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region, plus state-by-year fixed effects and city fixed effects. I will cluster standard errors at the state level, report first‑stage F statistics, and run balance, placebo (pre‑1990), and overidentification/falsification tests (including checks that audit_grant does not predict other municipal inputs). The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the grant affected local spending or economic conditions through channels other than segregation (e.g., nonprofit activity, measurement or follow‑up differences), or if the instrument is weak; I will report sensitivity analyses and, if exclusion is doubtful, present bounds and reduced‑form estimates. If audit_grant fails robustness checks I will not claim a causal IV estimate and will rely on fixed‑effects and difference‑in‑differences robustness checks instead.

CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | plausible
waterways | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate the causal effect with a fuzzy IV panel design that uses the 1990 randomized fair‑housing testing grant as an instrument for city segregation and implements 2SLS with city fixed effects and state‑by‑year fixed effects to absorb time‑invariant city heterogeneity and common shocks. The first stage will regress the multigroup entropy segregation index on audit_grant interacted with a post‑1990 indicator (to capture the grant’s post‑assignment impact), plus controls and fixed effects; the second stage will regress direct general expenditure per resident on the predicted segregation from the first stage. Key variables are the segregation index (treatment), direct general expenditure per resident (outcome), audit_grant × post indicator (instrument), and controls log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate and region. I will report first‑stage F‑statistics, conduct event‑study/pre‑trend tests around 1990, and show OLS and IV estimates with robust and clustered standard errors. The main threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the grant directly affected municipal spending through channels other than segregation (e.g., local civic mobilization, information or funding spillovers) or if drawn and control cities experienced differential post‑1990 trends unrelated to segregation.

CANDIDATES:
waterways | violated
audit_grant | plausible
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate the causal effect using audit_grant — the 1990 randomized draw that funded third‑party fair‑housing audits — as an instrument for later city segregation and implement two‑stage least squares (effectively a fuzzy difference‑in‑differences across census waves) with state-by-year fixed effects and controls for log_pop to isolate exogenous variation in segregation. Key variables are: instrument = audit_grant, treatment = multigroup entropy segregation index (0–100), outcome = direct general expenditure per resident (dollars), with additional covariates pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate and region to improve precision. I will test first‑stage strength, report IV (LATE) estimates and compare with within‑city fixed‑effects OLS; I will also run placebo and balance tests using pre‑1990 outcomes and demographic trends to assess the randomization. The principal remaining threat is violation of the exclusion restriction — the grant could have altered local public spending through channels other than segregation (e.g., community organizing, migration, or local nonprofit activity) or instrument weakness if the grant only weakly shifted segregation; I will probe this with heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses.  
CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | plausible
waterways | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I will estimate the causal effect of racial segregation on city per‑resident direct general expenditure using the 1990 randomized fair‑housing testing grant (audit_grant) as an instrument for the city segregation index in a two‑stage least squares design that exploits the exogenous random draw and its impact in post‑1990 census years.  In the first stage I instrument the multigroup entropy segregation index (0–100) with audit_grant interacted with post‑1990 indicators (or restrict to post‑1990 observations) plus controls and state‑by‑year fixed effects to capture the documented ~2.2 point downstream effect; in the second stage I regress per‑resident direct general expenditure (real dollars) on the instrumented segregation index.  I will control for log_pop, pct_black, pct_hisp, med_income, own_rate, region and include state‑by‑year fixed effects, and cluster standard errors at the state (or metropolitan) level.  I will test relevance (first‑stage F), run placebo tests on pre‑1990 trends, and report ITT estimates alongside IV to show robustness.  The primary threat is violation of the exclusion restriction if the grant changed municipal spending or reporting directly (e.g., by prompting local policy responses, enforcement changes, or differential data entry) rather than only reducing segregation; I will assess this with balance tests on observables and checks for changes in outcomes unlikely to be affected by segregation.  
CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | plausible
waterways | violated
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant
